questions.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Circle
questions.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ traversed from the point $(0,-4)$ to the point $(4,0)$ in the fourth quadrant?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066920/assets/0baaafbe9846ccef2c06a3b1a86eccac394344afc2dfd94bba2907ebb1cf2362.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{e}^{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot 4\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Line Integral of a Function Over a Circle
questions.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\sqrt[3]{y+1}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $6$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{36({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\sqrt[3]{y+1},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt[3]{6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt[3]{6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1}\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt[3]{6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1,$ $\text{d}u=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt[3]{6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t & =6{\int }_{1}^{1}\sqrt[3]{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6(0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=y\,\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ traversed from the point $(0,2)$ to the point $(-2,0)$ in the second quadrant?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066920/assets/d0ae53dd5d0932cbf834a166e851c227f75cb546b591a9fd43930ec06f0e9ddf.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=y\,\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\sqrt{4-(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\sqrt{4-4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(0,-2)$ in the third quadrant?
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066920/assets/1fd6c2df8b8467a46ed36b515842b88656883733376ee732839bab4085ca019c.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =8{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}8{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Line Integral of a Function Over a Circle
questions.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=2x-3$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2x-3,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-3 \\  & =3(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\,\text{d}t & =9[2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =9[2(0-0)-(2\pi -0)] \\  & =-18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
